ingredients: 1 small can (6 oz) Cento tomato paste
1/4 cup water, or a splash to loosen
1 tsp salt, plus more to taste
1/4 cup red wine, or a splash
red-sauce.notes:
The longer this cooks, the better it gets. 20 to 30 minutes is the minimum; if you've got an hour or two, let it go low and slow with the lid cracked, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if it gets too thick.\n\nThe rosemary-and-fennel oil is the base of the flavor. The rosemary comes out after a few minutes so it doesn't go bitter; the fennel stays.

Amounts for the oil, fennel, Italian seasoning, salt, and water are starting points. Adjust to taste, especially the salt.

The onion and garlic are optional. With them it's a fuller sauce; without, it's faster and cleaner-tasting. Both are good.

Meat version: brown 1 to 2 Italian sausages first and deglaze with a splash of wine (red), then build the sauce on top of that. If the sausage left a lot of fat in the pot, either pour some of it off or use less olive oil in the next step.
steps: For the meat version, start here: brown the sausage in the dry pot over medium heat, breaking it up, until it's got color and the fat has rendered. Deglaze with a splash of wine (red is best), scraping up the browned bits, and let it cook off for a minute. Push the sausage to the side or scoop it out, then continue with the oil below. Skip this step for the plain sauce.

Warm the olive oil in the pot over medium-low heat. Add the rosemary sprig and the fennel seeds and cook lightly for a few minutes, until the oil smells like rosemary. Pull the rosemary out; leave the fennel in.
If you're using the onion and garlic, add them now and cook, stirring, until soft, about 5 minutes.

Add the whole can of tomato paste. Stir it into the oil and keep cooking, stirring often, until it darkens a shade and smells sweet, about 3 to 5 minutes. Browning the paste is what gives the sauce its depth, so don't rush this.
Pour in both cans of sauce and a splash of water to cut it. Start with about 1/4 cup and add more if it's thicker than you want. If you browned sausage, return it to the pot now.

Add the Italian seasoning and a decent amount of salt. Simmer, partly covered, for 20 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then. Taste near the end and add more salt until it pops; it needs more than you think.
red-sauce.title: Red Sauce

ingredients: 1/2 cup brewed espresso or strong coffee, cooled
tiramisu.notes:
This only makes ONE layer. If you want the classic two-layer tiramisu, double everything.

Plan ahead: it needs at least 4 hours in the fridge, and it's better the next day.

Use the hard Savoiardi ladyfingers, not the soft cake-style ones; the soft ones turn to mush. Keep the yolks and mascarpone cold until you use them.
steps: Set up a double boiler: fill a saucepan with 1 to 2 inches of simmering water and set a heatproof bowl on top. The bottom of the bowl shouldn't touch the water.
In that bowl, whisk the egg yolks and powdered sugar constantly for about 8 to 10 minutes until the mixture is thick, pale, and reaches about 160°F (71°C). This pasteurizes the eggs.
Remove from heat and let the bowl cool for 5 minutes, whisking occasionally so a crust doesn't form.
Gently mix in the mascarpone with a spatula or a mixer on low until smooth and creamy. Don't overmix or it can curdle.
Brew the espresso or strong coffee and let it cool completely.
Quickly dip each ladyfinger into the coffee, about 1 second per side. Don't soak them; just lightly coat.

Arrange the dipped ladyfingers in a single layer in your dish and spread the mascarpone mixture over them. As written, that's one layer. If you doubled the recipe, repeat with a second layer of ladyfingers and cream.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight for the best flavor and texture.
Just before serving, dust the top with the cocoa powder through a fine sieve.

ingredients: 3/4 tsp dried oregano, plus more for the end
8 oz fresh mozzarella, torn into chunks
baked-gnocchi-tomato-cream.notes:
Gnocchi in a garlicky tomato-cream sauce, topped with mozzarella and parm and broiled until bubbly. Needs an oven-safe skillet (cast iron or stainless, no plastic handle).

The salt, pepper, and oregano in the ingredient list are a starting point, not the total. Season as you go and taste at every stage, especially after the cream goes in and again once the gnocchi are tossed. The late-stage salt, pepper, and oregano are make or break for this dish; the oregano you put in the oil at the start fades, so it needs a second hit near the end.

Grating the tomatoes replaces blanching and peeling. Basil goes in at the end so it stays fresh instead of frying in the oil. 1 cup of cream is on the light side for 2 lb of gnocchi; go to 1 1/2 cups if you want it saucier.
steps: Cut the Roma tomatoes in half and grate the cut side on a box grater over a bowl until only the skin is left in your hand; discard the skins. (This replaces blanching and peeling, same result, way less work.) Put a large pot of water on to boil and salt it heavily; it should taste like the ocean.

In a large oven-safe skillet over low heat, add the olive oil, the rosemary sprig, thyme, oregano, chili flakes, salt, and pepper. Let it warm gently for 5 minutes so the herbs flavor the oil. It should not sizzle hard. The rosemary is a big part of the flavor, but pull the sprig out after a few minutes, once the oil smells like it, or it turns bitter and woody.
Raise heat to medium. Add the onion and garlic and cook, stirring often, until the onion is soft and translucent, about 10 minutes. Don't let the garlic brown.

Pour the grated tomato into the pan and simmer until it thickens and the raw smell is gone, about 5 minutes. Taste it and add salt and pepper if it's flat; you'll season again later, so get it close but don't go all the way yet.
Drop the gnocchi into the boiling water. They're done as soon as they float to the top, usually 2 to 3 minutes. Drain. Set your oven broiler to high now.

Stir the cream into the skillet and simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens slightly. Now taste for real: the cream mutes everything, so this is where the salt, pepper, and oregano matter most. The oregano from the start has faded by now; add a fresh pinch or two, stir, taste, and repeat with all three until it tastes right on its own. If the sauce is bland here, the whole dish will be.

Add the drained gnocchi and the torn basil to the sauce and toss until every piece is coated. Taste one gnocchi with sauce on it and do a final salt, pepper, and oregano check; the gnocchi soak up seasoning. Scatter the mozzarella and parmesan evenly over the top.

Slide the skillet under the broiler, about 6 inches from the heat, until the cheese is melted and browned in spots, 3 to 5 minutes. Watch it; broilers go from golden to burnt fast. Let it rest a couple minutes before serving. The handle will be hot.
baked-gnocchi-tomato-cream.title: Baked Gnocchi in Tomato Cream Sauce
